opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that the improvement has been really large, but it's a bit hard to pin down precisely, because a lot of it doesn't come from the base model in isolation. It comes from the whole stack: better post-training, better scaffolding, better tool use, and models that have been trained specifically on agentic tasks.

When GPT-4 first came out, if you tried to get it to do a nontrivial software engineering task autonomously, where it has a repo, has to run commands, read the errors, and iterate, it would mostly flail. It could write a function that looked plausible. But it would get stuck in loops, lose track of what it was doing, or confidently claim it had fixed something it hadn't. On agentic benchmarks of that era, it was solving a pretty small fraction of realistic tasks.

Since then, if you look at things like the METR-style measurements of how long a task an AI can complete with some reasonable reliability, the trend has been something like a doubling every several months. That compounds really fast. You go from tasks that take a human a few minutes to tasks that take a human an hour or more, and the frontier keeps moving out.

I'd add some caveats. Benchmarks overstate things in some ways. The tasks tend to be well specified and self-contained, and they have clean automatic checks. Real engineering work is messier. You have to figure out what the actual problem is, deal with huge codebases, coordinate with people, and make judgment calls about tradeoffs. Models are still noticeably weaker there than the headline numbers suggest. But I also don't think it's purely benchmark gaming. If you talk to engineers who use these tools day to day, the qualitative shift is pretty clear. Models went from autocomplete-plus to something you can actually hand a moderately sized, well-scoped task and expect it to come back done a decent fraction of the time.

So my overall take is that it's been one of the fastest-improving capability areas. I take that seriously as a leading indicator, because software engineering, and especially AI research engineering, is exactly the kind of work where automation could feed back into accelerating AI progress itself.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think this is actually a pretty interesting case, because the underlying model has been roughly the same — or at least the headline name has been the same — but the agentic performance has gone up quite a lot. And I think there are a few different things going on there that are worth separating.

So one thing is just that the model has actually been updated. GPT-4 at initial release, then GPT-4 Turbo, then the various 4o versions — these are different models, with more post-training, probably different data mixes, and in some cases they were specifically trained to be better at things like tool use and following multi-step instructions. So part of the improvement is just that OpenAI made the model better at this. It's not purely a scaffolding story.

But then the other big thing is the scaffolding and elicitation. When GPT-4 first came out, people were mostly just prompting it in a chat window, and the early agent attempts — AutoGPT and that sort of thing — were honestly pretty bad. They'd get stuck in loops, they'd lose track of what they were doing, they'd hallucinate that they'd completed a task. And a lot of what's happened since then is that people have figured out how to structure the problem: give the model a proper tool interface, let it actually run code and see the output, let it iterate on errors, give it a reasonable way to manage context over a long task. On something like SWE-bench, you can see this really clearly — the same base model with a better agent harness goes from basically not working to solving a nontrivial fraction of real GitHub issues.

So if you ask me to decompose it, I'd say a decent chunk of the gain is "we got better at using the model," and a decent chunk is "the model got better." And it's genuinely hard to pull those apart cleanly, because the improved models were partly trained to work well with the kinds of scaffolds people were building.

I think the thing I'd flag as important here is that this makes evals tricky. If you evaluated GPT-4 in March 2023 and concluded it couldn't do much agentic stuff, that conclusion was somewhat about the model and somewhat about how much effort anyone had put into eliciting the capability. And that gap — between what you measure at release and what people can get out of it a year later — is something you really have to account for if you're trying to make safety-relevant claims about what a model can and can't do. I don't think the gap is unbounded; I think there's a real sense in which the capabilities were latent and we were under-eliciting. But I'd be cautious about how much of a model's future performance you can predict from the initial release numbers.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s been a pretty substantial improvement, but it’s hard to disentangle improvements in the model from improvements in how people use it. You can take the same underlying model and get quite different results depending on the tools you give it, how you structure the task, and whether it can run tests and iterate on its mistakes.

And there’s a distinction between being good at individual steps and being able to reliably complete a whole task. It might write a useful function or diagnose a bug, but then get stuck somewhere in a longer sequence and fail to recover. So I’d want to look at how often it completes realistic tasks end to end, with a fixed amount of human assistance, rather than just whether its code looks better.

My qualitative impression is that the overall systems have gotten meaningfully more capable. I’d be more cautious about attributing all of that to improvements in GPT-4 itself.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s improved substantially, but it’s tricky to disentangle improvements in the underlying model from improvements in how people use it. If you compare an agent built around GPT-4 when it first came out with a good agent now, you’re changing the scaffolding, the tools it has access to, the prompting, and potentially how much compute you’re spending on each task.

Software engineering is particularly sensitive to those things, because you can run tests, look at the errors, and iterate. A model that doesn’t reliably produce the right patch on its first attempt might still be useful if you give it a good setup for doing that iteration.

So I’d distinguish “How much better has GPT-4 itself gotten?” from “How much better are the systems we can build with GPT-4?” I’m more confident that the latter has improved a lot. And that’s relevant for forecasting: even if the underlying models stopped improving, I’d still expect people to get better at turning their existing capabilities into useful work.
